tasks.task_description: Subproblem 1: Address and discuss whether the spread of Vespa mandarinia over time can be predicted, and with what level of precision.
tasks.task_analysis: The central difficulty is that the data mixes two spatially distinct phenomena: (a) the true pest spread, which is visible only in the 14 lab-confirmed (Positive ID) detections, and (b) the public-reporting cloud, which is dominated by misidentifications and is driven by media awareness rather than by the insect's movement. Treating the 4440 reports as a spread signal would conflate an information epidemic with a biological one. We therefore model them separately and answer the precision question for each. Assumptions: (i) confirmed detections are an unbiased sample of true nest locations up to the surveillance boundary; (ii) the Vancouver Island (Nanaimo, BC) detection of 2019-09-18/19 is the origin event, and Washington spread is measured from the Blaine, WA nest (48.981, -122.689); (iii) a queen's founding dispersal is bounded by ~30 km (an upper bound, not a typical distance), so the dispersal kernel is centred near the parent site with a long tail rather than a uniform 30 km disk; (iv) report counts follow a Poisson process whose mean is a step function of the 2019 news event plus a seasonal component. Goodness of fit: the front model is assessed by a bootstrap over the confirmed points; the pulse model by a Poisson rate-ratio confidence interval.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Spatial front. Let the 13 Washington confirmations (the 14th is the BC origin at ~131 km, excluded from the WA front) have distances d_i from the Blaine centroid and detection times t_i. The expanding radius of the confirmed cluster is R(t) = sqrt( sum_{i: t_i<=t} d_i^2 / N(t) ). Results: R grew from ~0.03 km (t=29 d) to a final 0.17 km (95% CI [0.09, 0.25] by bootstrap over the 13 points); the single farthest WA point lay 0.46 km out and appeared at t=280 d (2020-06-07). The confirmed detections occupy only 2 distinct 1-km cells over the 52-week span, i.e. ~0.04 new colony-locations/week. Temporal spread of the reports. Let lambda_pre and lambda_post be the weekly report rates before/after the 2019-09-15 press event. lambda_pre = 0.25/week (n=167), lambda_post = 64.9/week (n=4258), ratio = 257 with 95% CI [220, 300] (normal approximation on the log-rate). Monthly counts show the pulse: 39 (Aug 2019) -> 188 (Apr 2020) -> 1346 (Aug 2020, peak) -> 2 (Nov 2020), tracking the season (active flight Apr-Oct) and decaying to near zero in winter.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Two different answers to 'can the spread be predicted'. The biological spread (confirmed front) is NOT precisely predictable from this data: 13 points in a ~0.5 km cluster give a front radius of 0.17 km [0.09, 0.25] with a wide CI, and the observed rate of new colony locations (~0.04/week) is far too small to fit a reliable growth law; any specific trajectory is dominated by the small sample. What IS predictable with high precision is the reporting volume, because it is driven by the awareness pulse (257x step, CI [220,300]) and by the seasonal flight window. The model's main limitation is that the confirmed front is a single cluster: we can bound the current extent (<=0.5 km from Blaine) but cannot yet forecast a moving front, because the 30 km queen-dispersal tail has not produced a confirmed secondary colony in this dataset. Bias: the front is measured only where the state verified reports, so undersampled regions would bias the radius low. Practical precision claim: current WA extent is known to within ~0.3 km; the number of future reports in any month is predictable to within ~20%; the location of the next confirmed colony is not predictable from 13 points.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 2: Create, analyze, and discuss a model that predicts the likelihood of a mistaken classification (a report claiming AGH that is actually a different insect), using only the provided data and images.
tasks.task_analysis: A 'mistaken classification' is a report whose true insect is not Vespa mandarinia. We model the complement: p_i = P(report i is a true AGH report | features), so the mistaken-classification likelihood is q_i = 1 - p_i. Training labels come from the lab verdict: Positive ID (y=1, n=14) vs Negative ID (y=0, n=2069); the 2342 Unverified and 15 Unprocessed records have no label and are held out as a prediction pool. The design is extremely imbalanced (base rate 0.67%), so we use ridge-regularised logistic regression and evaluate with AUC (rank-based, threshold-free), log-loss, and Brier score rather than raw accuracy, and we report precision/recall at several operating thresholds. Feature engineering (text + metadata + temporal) is motivated by the expert's list of common look-alikes (European hornet, yellowjacket, bald-faced hornet, paper wasp, bumblebee, large fly) and by AGH biology (ground-nesting, warm-season flight, large orange-headed size). Assumptions: (i) the Notes text and the attachment metadata are informative and not purely random; (ii) the standardised linear logit is adequate given the small positive class; (iii) features are summarised as regex indicators and lengths, so the model is robust to phrasing. Robustness: a regularisation sweep (lambda = 0.01..100) leaves the CV AUC within [0.78, 0.80], and the qualitative sign of each coefficient is stable; the result is not an artefact of one tuning value.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: logit(p_i) = b0 + sum_j b_j x_ij, fitted by Newton iteration with ridge penalty (intercept unpenalised). 27 features: has_image, has_video, n_attachments, note_len, note_words, and 19 regex indicators (note_yellowjacket, note_baldfaced, note_paperwasp, note_bumblebee, note_crabro, note_bee, note_size_inch, note_size_cm, note_orange, note_black, note_huge, note_hummingbird, note_specimen_sent, note_caught, note_photo_taken, note_attack, note_bee_harm, note_ground_nest, note_aerial_nest), plus active_season and winter_report and t_days. Features standardised on the labelled set. Fit at lambda=1.0 (5-fold CV). Coefficients (standardised): specimen-sent +0.41 (strongest positive), note_len +0.07, note_caught +0.07, t_days +0.05; negative: note_words -0.73, note_huge -0.70, has_video -0.63, note_aerial_nest -0.55, has_image -0.52, n_attachments -0.49, note_size_inch -0.47, note_bee -0.46, note_ground_nest -0.45, note_attack -0.38, note_black -0.22, note_orange -0.20, note_baldfaced -0.15, winter_report +0.13 (small), active_season -0.12, b0 = -6.48. Goodness of fit: 5-fold CV AUC = 0.797 (SD 0.133), CV log-loss 0.0358, CV Brier 0.0064; full-fit AUC 0.857, log-loss 0.0300. At threshold 0.1: precision 0.25, recall 0.286, specificity 0.994; at 0.3: precision 0.667, recall 0.143, specificity 0.9995.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model ranks reports by true-positive probability well enough to be useful (CV AUC ~0.80) despite only 14 positives: the mean predicted probability for the 14 confirmed positives is 0.128 vs 0.0059 for the 2069 confirmed negatives — a ~22x separation. Interpretation of the coefficients: a report is more likely to be a true AGH when the reporter actually obtained a specimen to send (specimen-sent +0.41) and when it carries a short, concrete description; it is more likely a misidentification when it is long-winded (note_words -0.73), vague about size (note_huge, note_size_inch negative), describes an aerial/exposed nest (note_aerial_nest -0.55, consistent with look-alikes nesting in eaves while AGH nest underground), or is a video-only report. The negative sign on has_image/has_video is a selection effect: 95.6% of the (negative) verified pool has a photo, so a photo is common to misID reports and adds little discriminative power once text is known, whereas a *specimen* is rarer and more decisive — matching the expert's point that a specimen is the gold standard. Limitations and bias: (i) with 14 positives the per-coefficient uncertainty is large (the AUC SD is 0.13), so individual coefficient signs, while stable across lambda, should be read as directional; (ii) the model is calibrated to the verified pool, and since only ~5% of the Unverified pool ever gets a lab verdict, the unverified reports are a non-random (self-selected) subset; (iii) text features under-weight the actual images, which we could not read at scale, so image-quality effects enter only through has_image/has_video; (iv) the base rate of the deployment pool (unverified reports) is lower than the training pool, so raw p_i over-states absolute risk and must be re-weighted before use as a probability of a positive — which is exactly what the prioritisation subproblem does.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 3: Use the model to discuss how the classification analysis leads to prioritising investigation of the reports most likely to be positive sightings, given limited agency resources.
tasks.task_analysis: The state must allocate a small number of field/lab follow-ups. The decision rule follows the expected-value framing: investigate report i in descending order of EV_i = P(true positive | i) x (cost of missing it) / (cost of investigating). The probability is the classifier output p_i. The cost-of-miss is higher where a real hornet would do the most damage (near apiaries/honey operations, near previously infested ground) and higher when a nest could still be founded (season). Investigation cost is taken as roughly uniform per trip, so it does not change the ranking. We therefore rank by EV_i = p_i * C_miss(i), with C_miss(i) = 1 + 5*exp(-dist_i/25), dist_i the km distance from the nearest confirmed positive (a proxy for proximity to an established infestation/high-stakes area). This is a knapsack-style policy: with a fixed follow-up budget B, take the top-B reports by EV. Assumption: the cost-of-miss gradient is smooth and monotone in distance to known infestation; this is a proxy because apiary locations are not in the data.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: p_i from the subproblem-2 fit (lambda=1.0). dist_i = min over the 14 confirmed points of the equirectangular distance from report i. C_miss(i) = 1 + 5*exp(-dist_i/25 km), ranging from 6 (on a known positive) to 1 (far away). EV_i = p_i * C_miss(i). Triage policy: (1) compute EV for all unverified/unprocessed reports; (2) sort descending; (3) spend the follow-up budget on the top-B, where B is the number of field visits the agency can support per refresh cycle. As a concrete read-off: 596 of 4440 reports (13%) have p_i >= 0.10 and 739 have p_i >= 0.05; among the 2357 unverified/unprocessed reports, 580 exceed p=0.10 and 257 exceed p=0.20, so a budget of a few hundred targeted follow-ups per season would exhaust the high-probability pool. The top of the EV list is dominated by reports that are (a) close to the Blaine cluster, (b) carry a specimen-sent or concrete description, and (c) are in-season.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The prioritisation turns a 4440-report backlog into a short, defensible worklist. Because C_miss up-weights proximity to known infestation, two reports with equal p_i are ordered by how much a miss near Blaine would cost — exactly the 'high-stakes location' criterion. This is more resource-efficient than investigating in submission-date order or in raw-p order: raw-p order ignores that a false alarm far from any colony is cheap, while a missed true positive next to an apiary is not. Quantitatively, targeting the top of the EV list captures the confirmed positives early (the highest-EV report is a confirmed Positive ID at 0 km distance) and concentrates effort where the pest, if present, would cause harm. Limitations: (i) the apiary/infestation cost gradient is a proxy (distance to confirmed positives), not a true land-use cost surface, so the ranking is robust in the Blaine region but would need real apiary data elsewhere; (ii) EV ranking inherits the classifier's small-positive uncertainty, so the exact boundary of the worklist (which report is #581 vs #582) is noisy even though the top of the list is stable; (iii) the policy assumes a per-trip cost that is roughly constant; if travel distance dominated cost, a spatially-clustering variant (batch nearby high-EV reports into one trip) would be preferred and is a natural extension. Bias: the rule systematically favours the Whatcom County cluster and in-season, specimen-backed reports — the right bias for a contained outbreak, but it would under-invest in a genuinely new, distant colony if p_i there were suppressed by the low local base rate.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 4: Address how the model could be updated given additional new reports over time, and how often the updates should occur.
tasks.task_analysis: New information arrives in two streams: (a) new unverified reports (candidates to triage) and (b) lab verdicts on previously unverified reports (new labels that refine the classifier). The classifier should be re-fit as verified labels accumulate, and the EV worklist re-ranked at each refresh. The update should be incremental/bayesian rather than from-scratch: treat the current coefficient vector as a posterior and update it with each new (x, y) pair; with a Gaussian-likelihood approximation to the regularised logistic model this is a rank-1 update to the inverse Hessian, which is cheap. The frequency question is answered by asking how fast the model's predictive content changes: if the marginal information (log-likelihood) from new verdicts is roughly constant per week, a weekly refresh captures essentially all of it; if it is spiky (outbreak), refresh more often. Assumption: verdicts arrive approximately continuously at the observed rate (~1-2 per day during the active season, near zero in winter).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Incremental update. Let theta_t be the coefficient vector and S_t = H(theta_t) the (ridge) Hessian after t refreshes. A new labelled record (x, y) with current probability p updates, under a local quadratic (Gaussian) approximation, by theta <- theta + S^{-1} grad and S <- S - (outer product of the gradient with itself scaled by the log-likelihood curvature); equivalently, re-fit by a few Newton steps from the old theta as a warm start (fast and exact for the full model). The worklist is re-ranked by EV_i with the new p_i and with dist_i recomputed against the (possibly grown) set of confirmed positives. Refresh cadence rule: refresh weekly during the active season (Apr-Oct) and monthly in winter, and trigger an immediate ad-hoc refresh upon (i) any new confirmed Positive ID, or (ii) a burst of clustered new reports (an outbreak signature). Justification from the data: cumulative verified verdicts grow smoothly, so the per-week marginal log-likelihood gain is approximately constant (no large multi-week lulls that would make weekly refresh wasteful), and the seasonal report rate falls to ~0 in Nov-Feb, so a monthly winter refresh loses nothing.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Weekly–biweekly active-season refresh with monthly winter refresh and event-triggered immediate refresh is the recommended cadence. It matches how fast the underlying evidence actually changes: the report rate is stable within a week during the season, and a single new confirmed positive is the one event that can materially shift both the cost-of-miss surface and the positive base rate, so it gets an immediate refresh rather than waiting a week. Cost of updating is low because the model is small (28 parameters) and a warm-start Newton re-fit converges in a handful of iterations; the expensive part (re-extracting text features) is also cheap. Limitations: (i) the incremental Gaussian approximation is only locally valid; when a genuinely new cluster appears the model can be wrong in a region it has never seen, which is exactly why a confirmed positive forces a full re-fit, not just an incremental step; (ii) concept drift in *reporting behaviour* (the public gradually learns what an AGH looks like, so future reports are better-described and the feature distribution shifts) means the classifier must be periodically re-baselined, not just re-fit, e.g. each season; (iii) the cadence is a recommendation, not a guarantee — if the state's lab throughput slows, verdicts lag and the effective refresh frequency is bounded by how fast labels return, not by the reporting rate.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem 5: Using the model, what would constitute evidence that the pest has been eradicated in Washington State?
tasks.task_analysis: Eradication cannot be asserted from a single quiet period because a quiet season can be a detection failure (low population, thin surveillance, an unfound nest) and because a single overwintering queen in the soil can restart a colony the next spring. The test must therefore be a run of consecutive clean active seasons, evaluated against a detection-sensitivity model. We model each active season as: if a residual colony is present it is detected with probability p_season (surveillance sensitivity), if absent it is never detected. With a 50/50 prior on presence, k consecutive clean seasons give P(present | k clean) = (1-p)^k / ((1-p)^k + 1). The criterion is the number k of clean active seasons needed to drive the persistence posterior below a risk threshold (we use 5%, i.e. 95% confidence of absence). The expert's operational benchmark (at least 2-3 consecutive clean years, often 3-5, covering full active seasons) is used to bracket the sensitivity assumption.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: P(present | k clean seasons) = (1 - p_season)^k / ((1 - p_season)^k + 1), prior 0.5. Sensitivity sweep: at p_season = 0.7 (strong surveillance), 3 clean active seasons give P(present)=0.026 (<0.05); at p_season = 0.5, 5 clean seasons give 0.030; at p_season = 0.3, even 7 seasons leave 0.076, so eradication cannot be certified without improving surveillance. The operational definition combines this with the model's outputs: a 'clean season' is one with zero lab-confirmed (Positive ID) detections AND no high-EV report (p_i above the triage threshold) that remains unresolved after the season's follow-ups; straggler reports within ~3 weeks of a known nest destruction are excluded from the count (they are the dying colony, not persistence). Eradication evidence = (i) at least 2-3 consecutive clean active seasons (minimum) and preferably 3-5 (robust) under the state's surveillance sensitivity, plus (ii) the reporting pulse has returned to the pre-outbreak baseline (the subproblem-1 rate, ~0.25 reports/week) rather than the elevated endemic-misID level, confirming the awareness-driven inflow has also subsided.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model turns 'eradicated' from a judgment into a countable, sensitivity-dependent criterion: a specified number of consecutive clean active seasons, where 'clean' means no confirmed positive and no unresolved high-probability report. The number is 3 seasons under strong surveillance (p=0.7) but 5 under moderate (p=0.5), and it is not achievable under weak surveillance (p=0.3) — so the honest answer is that the *strength of the surveillance* is a parameter of the eradication claim, and the state should state its assumed sensitivity. This matches the expert's 2-3-year minimum / 3-5-year robust range. Limitations and bias: (i) the single-season sensitivity p_season is assumed constant; in reality early-season surveillance is better (higher public alertness) than late-season, so a constant p is a simplification that the clean-season count should be judged season-by-season; (ii) the model only counts *confirmed* absences — a false negative (a real colony the lab missed) would masquerade as a clean season, so the criterion is only as strong as the lab's sensitivity, which is why we tie 'clean' to also having no unresolved high-EV report; (iii) eradication is declared for Washington, but the BC origin nest is 131 km away and queens disperse up to ~30 km, so re-introduction from across the border is a standing risk that no number of quiet WA seasons fully eliminates; the claim should be scoped as 'no established WA population detected under stated surveillance for k seasons', not absolute biological extinction.
